newsitem.title: USA: NY state panel moves ahead on pay-to-play rule.
newsitem.headline: NY state panel moves ahead on pay-to-play rule.

text.p: New York State judicial officials have decided to proceed with development of a rule endorsed by the New York City bar that would curb pay-to-play by lawyers in the state that have municipal bond practices, a prominent New York City bond lawyer said.

"The (New York State) Administrative Board met last week. I'm told it was the longest meeting in the history of the board," William Josephson, an official with the Association of the Bar of the City of New York said at a meeting of the American Bar Association's business law section in Boston on Saturday.

"I'm told that (Administrative Board) staff has now been designated to work with the (New York) City bar to develop a rule that would be subject to further consideration by the Administrative Board," said Josephson, who headed a city bar association panel that drafted the pay-to-play ban adopted by the city bar last year.

Pay-to-play refers to bond professionals that give contributions to elected municipal officials in return for bond business. Municipal bond dealers have adopted voluntary curbs on the practice, but bond lawyers have resisted repeated requests by federal regulators to take similar action.

Josephson could not predict the final outcome of the state board's review. "The next step is that they could decide not to issue" the draft rule, he said. "(Or) they could amend it. They might decide to hold a public hearing. They could promulgate the rule tomorrow if they wanted. It's up to them."

The New York City bar's rule generally is modeled after the Municipal Securities Rulemaking Board's three-year-old "pay-to- play" rule G-37, which bars muni dealers that make contributions to issuer clients from engaging in negotiated bond business for two years with those governments.

But the city bar's rule would go considerably further by applying not only to contributions to issuer officials but "solicitations" resulting in contributions. It also would cover "soft money" contributions to some political groups.

The city bar on March 10 urged the state's Administrative Board to adopt the controversial rule for all lawyers in the state. The board is a five-member panel that includes the chief judge of the state's court of appeals and judges from four appellate divisions that set disciplinary standards for the state's thousands of lawyers.
The city bar also will urge the ABA at its annual meeting in August to recommend that each state adopt the policy.
Key ABA panel members at the Boston meeting openly differed over whether to adopt the standard.
